subject: physics
question_text: Will a pendulum clock gain or lose time when taken to the top of a mountain?

verification.note: The mark split is invented and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The question itself is sourced, not invented.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: What happens to g
lines: The value of g decreases as we go higher above
the surface of the earth. So g at the top of a
mountain is a little less than g at sea level.
steps.why: g falls off with height because the place is further from the centre of the earth.

recall.must_convey: That g is smaller at the top of a mountain than at sea level.
accept: g is less on the mountain

steps.memory_tip: At the top of Everest g is about 9.78 m s⁻², against 9.8 at sea level.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that g is smaller up there before using the formula.

steps.label: What the clock does
lines: T = 2π√(l/g), so T ∝ 1/√g. A smaller g gives a
LONGER time period — each swing now takes

lines.text: The clock runs slow — it LOSES time

steps.why: A pendulum clock counts swings, so a longer swing means fewer counts in a real hour.
common_mistakes: Saying it gains time because the bob is "lighter" up there — the mass of the bob does not appear in the period.

recall.must_convey: That a smaller g gives a longer time period, so the clock runs slow and loses time.

steps.memory_tip: A slower swing always means a slow clock: up a mountain, down a mine, or on a longer string.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write T ∝ 1/√g, then the word LOSES.

insider_note: One word decides the second mark — write that the clock LOSES time, rather than leaving it to be read out of T ∝ 1/√g.
